reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Neurogenic bladder describes bladder dysfunction due to disease or injury of the nervous system, with the pattern depending on the level of the neurological lesion

Suprapontine and suprasacral (upper motor neuron) lesions typically cause a spastic, overactive detrusor, often with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, whereas sacral or peripheral (lower motor neuron) lesions cause a flaccid, areflexic, poorly emptying bladder
Common causes include spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, spina bifida, diabetes mellitus, Parkinson's disease, stroke, and cauda equina lesions
The paramount goal of management is protection of the upper urinary tracts, because high storage pressures and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia can cause hydronephrosis and renal failure
Video-urodynamics is central to characterising bladder behaviour, storage pressures, and sphincter coordination to guide safe management
Clean intermittent catheterisation is a cornerstone for bladders that do not empty adequately, reducing residual urine and infection risk while preserving the upper tracts

Management principles combine measures to lower storage pressure and improve emptying, such as antimuscarinics, intradetrusor botulinum toxin, catheterisation regimens, and, in selected cases, augmentation or diversion surgery
Patients are at risk of recurrent urinary infection, stones, and, in high spinal cord injuries, autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder distension
reference.pathophysiology: Normal micturition depends on coordinated control between the pontine micturition centre, spinal pathways, and sacral (S2-S4) reflexes governing the detrusor and urethral sphincter. Neurological lesions disrupt this coordination in patterns determined by lesion level. Upper motor neuron lesions above the sacral cord release the sacral reflex from higher inhibition, producing detrusor overactivity and often detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, in which the sphincter contracts against a contracting bladder, generating dangerously high pressures. Lower motor neuron or peripheral lesions abolish the reflex arc, producing an acontractile, flaccid bladder with retention and overflow. Sustained high intravesical pressure and incomplete emptying threaten the upper tracts and predispose to infection and stones.
additionalDifferentials: Detrusor overactivity from non-neurogenic causes (idiopathic overactive bladder)
Multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating disease
additionalInvestigations: Video-urodynamic studies to assess detrusor pressure, compliance, and sphincter coordination
Renal function tests and upper tract imaging (ultrasound) to monitor for hydronephrosis
Urinalysis and culture for infection surveillance
Neurological evaluation and imaging directed at the underlying condition
Periodic surveillance for bladder stones and, where relevant, malignancy in long-term catheterised patients
redFlags: High detrusor storage pressures or detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia threatening the upper tracts and renal function
New or progressive hydronephrosis and rising creatinine
Autonomic dysreflexia in high spinal cord injury, a potentially life-threatening emergency triggered by bladder overdistension
Urosepsis in an obstructed or poorly draining neurogenic bladder
Acute cauda equina syndrome presenting with retention and neurological deficit
reference.prognosis: With structured management focused on low-pressure storage, adequate emptying, and regular upper tract surveillance, many patients maintain renal function and continence; neglected high-pressure bladders carry a significant risk of progressive renal impairment and recurrent complications.
pitfalls: Focusing on continence while neglecting upper tract protection and storage pressures
Failing to recognise and treat detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia
Not anticipating autonomic dysreflexia during bladder distension or instrumentation in high spinal injuries
Inadequate surveillance for renal deterioration, stones, and infection
Treating overactivity with antimuscarinics without ensuring adequate emptying
